purpose: Quantified evidence of animal-study reduction, avoidance, or replacement. Metrics are kept separate from event chronology and regulatory-context records because a policy may exist without a measurable denominator or realized displacement.

metrics.regulator: US EPA Office of Pesticide Programs
metrics.context: Waiver of acute dermal toxicity tests for pesticide formulations
metrics.basis: EPA reported receiving approximately 200–300 dermal formulation toxicity tests annually and stated that each generally used 10 animals per test.
metrics.note: This is a mature study-waiver precedent rather than a human-model substitution. It is valuable as a benchmark for how an agency can translate regulatory streamlining into a quantitative animal-use estimate.

manuscript_impacts.claim: Adoption should ultimately be evaluated using measurable displacement rather than event counts alone

metrics.regulator: US EPA Office of Pesticide Programs
metrics.context: Acute dermal toxicity waiver requests under EPA's 2016 formulation and 2020 technical-chemical guidance
metrics.basis: Sum of EPA's annual reported acute-dermal waiver metrics: 31, 37, 30, 56, 61 and 47 waivers for FY2018-2023, with corresponding annual animal-reduction ranges.
metrics.note: Unlike the 2016 prospective estimate, this is observed agency tracking of granted waivers. The range reflects test-design-dependent animal use.

manuscript_impacts.claim: Regulators can and do track realized animal reductions from waiver policies

metrics.regulator: US EPA Office of Pesticide Programs
metrics.context: Branch-level pesticide acute-toxicity decisions using citations, bridging, waivers and weight-of-evidence rationales
metrics.basis: EPA reports that OPP registering divisions began capturing branch-level decisions where acute toxicity testing was not necessary; FY2023 metrics include data citations, bridging requests, additional study waivers and weight-of-evidence rationales.
metrics.note: This is currently one of the strongest public denominators in the corpus. It measures avoided testing across multiple evidence strategies, not exclusively human-based NAM substitution, so it should be used as a broader transition metric rather than a human-model count.

manuscript_impacts.claim: The transition can be measured at the decision level with both study and animal denominators
Public baselines and displacement metrics are feasible rather than merely aspirational

metrics.context: Omission of a two-year rat carcinogenicity study when an integrated weight-of-evidence assessment is sufficient under ICH S1B(R1)
metrics.basis: FDA/CDER/OND authors state that when a two-year rat study is not conducted, more than 400 animals will not be used, depending on study design.
metrics.note: This provides a useful per-decision conversion factor but not a national total because the number of actual S1B(R1) omissions is not supplied in the source.

manuscript_impacts.claim: A single evidence-based omission decision can have substantial animal-use consequences

metrics.context: Evaluation supporting use of the GHS mixtures equation for acute oral toxicity of covered pesticide formulations
metrics.basis: EPA states that the decision followed a comprehensive EPA/NIEHS analysis evaluating nearly 700 pesticide formulations.
metrics.note: This is not itself an animal-count displacement denominator. It quantifies the empirical base supporting an implemented computational alternative and should not be converted into animals avoided without further data.

manuscript_impacts.claim: Large retrospective datasets can support transition from validation to regulatory implementation
